title: TA8-00255
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXX XXXXX (the claimant), a citizen of the People's Republic of China, claims refugee protection pursuant to section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.

The claimant alleges that in XXXXX 2007, she was taken to an underground Christian church service by a friend. The underground church had between 20 to 30 members. The claimant did not pray nor study the Bible with other members each time she attended because the organizer would assign her other duties consisting of XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX before and after church services. On XXXXX, 2007, the organizer sent the claimant and three others to distribute flyers. When she returned to the private home where the church service was to be held, she saw seven to eight police cars. She also witnessed the arrest of church members. Being fearful, she went to a friend's home.

The claimant alleges that the Public Security Bureau (PSB) came to her home on the night of XXXXX, 2007, searching it and taking away her computer and papers, which were eventually returned to the claimant's mother. The PSB accused the claimant of being a member of the underground church, violation of religious regulations, distributing illegal flyers and disturbing social stability. The PSB visited a second time on XXXXX, 2007 and a third time on XXXXX, 2007. On the third visit, her mother was warned not to conceal the claimant otherwise she would be charged with harbouring a criminal. The PSB continue to search for the claimant at her mother's home and the claimant has learned that the organizer and four other members were sentenced on XXXXX, 2008. An additional 15 members were sent to labour re-education camps and two members were fined and released.
The claimant's identity as a national of the People's Republic of China is established by documentation1 provided to the Board by the claimant.

There were a number of credibility concerns. The claimant testified that there have been numerous visits by the PSB at her home with the intention of arresting her. There has never been an arrest warrant left at her home.

The documentation2 indicates: ... it is very common in China for the police authorities to leave a summons or subpoena with family members ( or possibly close friends, though that is probably less common), instructing them to pass it along to the person named on the summons. The person accepting the summons would be expected to sign an acknowledgment of receipt. This is not actually the proper procedure but it happens all the time, especially in cases where the person on the summons is not easily locatable... The panel prefers documentary evidence because it comes from knowledgeable sources that would reasonably be expected to know about such matters.

Further, given the alleged diligence with which they have pursued the claimant and that so many members were arrested and have been sentenced to significant punishment in detention and fined, it is reasonable to expect that if the authorities were seeking the claimant they would have issued an arrest warrant for her. The panel therefore determines, based on a balance of probabilities, that the authorities are not seeking the claimant.

The claimant testified to 22 members being arrested and long-term prison sentences and re-education through labour detentions, as well as fines. She was asked to comment on the lack of documentation concerning arrests in Fujian province. Her response was that she only knew that there was a raid and that the PSB came to her residence.

The panel has turned to the documentary evidence to ascertain the credibility of her allegation that the church meeting was raided and that the members were persecuted. With respect to the documentary evidence,3 Protestant worshippers number at least 20 million people in the official church and between 50 and 70 million in the non-state sanctioned churches. The website of the State Administration for Religious Affairs (SARA) states that family and friends holding meetings at home need not register with the government. However, there were many reports that police and officials of local Religious Affairs Bureaus (RABs) disrupted home worship meetings claiming that participants disturbed neighbours or social order or belonged to an "evil cult".4 The ability to hold meetings between family and friends and not need to register with authorities was confirmed in other documentation,5 which states that any gathering of believers with more than 40 is required by law to register with the government.

Documentation reveals that there is a large discrepancy in the treatment of house churches.6 In some parts of the country, unregistered house churches with hundreds of members meet openly with the full knowledge of local authorities who characterize the meetings as informal gatherings to pray, sing and study the Bible. In other areas, house church meetings of more than a handful of family members and friends are not permitted. House churches often encounter difficulties when there membership grows, when they arrange for the regular use of facilities for the specific purposes of conducting religious activities or when they forge links with other unregistered groups or with coreligionists overseas. Meetings of unregistered Protestants in small cities and rural areas may number in the hundreds.7 Documentation8 also highlights, "Protestant Christians who worshiped outside of government-approved venues or in their homes continue to face detention and abuse, especially for attempting to meet in large groups, traveling within and outside of the country for religious meetings, and otherwise holding peaceful religious assemblies in unregistered venues." The documentation9 also reported that unregistered religious groups experienced the most abuses and harassment in Anhui, Hebei, Henan, Shanxi, and Xinjiang provinces.

With respect to the situation of religious persecution within the claimant's province of Fujian, there is no persuasive information suggesting that religious persecution is occurring for groups that are as small as the claimant's. Although a number of different commentators have reported on the issue of religious persecution in China, one in particular, China Aid Association (CAA), stands out as being a significant source of up-to-date reporting and detailed accounts of harassment and repression of Protestant house churches in China.10 The report identifies four main targets of persecution: House church leaders, house churches in urban areas, Christian publications and foreign Christians and missionaries living and working in China. With respect to the claimant's particular circumstances, she testified that 22 members were arrested and long term prison sentences were imposed on the pastor and four others. Fifteen received re-education through labour for two and a half years and two had to pay fines. This is an example of an egregious situation where persons were arrested and would reasonably be expected to appear in reports dealing with religious persecution, not only from CAA but amongst the multitude of different resources which strive to inform the world of religious repression in China. Commentators have stated that the Chinese government has a "less antagonistic" attitude towards unregistered Protestants than it does towards unregistered Catholics, though it fears "house" churches may act as a cover for dissidents.11 What is clear to the panel is that in China, religious persecution of Protestant "house churches" does occur, however, it is not general in nature. Such factors as whether there are close links with the West, evangelisation, membership growth to become large-scale congregations, arrangements for regular use of facilities, whether an individual is a leader, rural or urban areas and location within China are all factors to consider.

The panel is mindful of the caveat that the number of persecution incidents is likely to be much higher because of censorship in communications12 and even considered the possibility that not all information is available to commentators. It concludes that since there is a significant amount of information detailing very specific examples from areas much more remote and difficult to access than Fujian, that it is reasonable for the panel to expect to see persuasive evidence that groups such as the claimant's, which are small and not required to register, are being raided and individuals being jailed in Fujian province.

Counsel provided documentation13 from a determination made by an Australian Tribunal where a citizen from Fujian was found to have protection rights. The panel is not bound by the decision of the Australian panel.

Given the totality of the documentary evidence which provides limited persuasive evidence that members of unregistered churches are being detained in Fujian province, the panel determines, based on a balance of probabilities, that members were not arrested by the PSB, nor are the authorities seeking to arrest the claimant.

With regard to the genuineness of Christian faith, the panel accepts that the claimant is a Christian practicing in Canada because of documentation14 presented but given the above analysis of the documentary evidence for Fujian province, the panel determines that the evidence does not support that there are "good grounds" for fearing persecution if the claimant were to practice her religion in an unregistered "house church" with which the claimant was associated prior to coming to Canada. In this particular claim, there is not a serious possibility that the claimant would be persecuted, or that she would be subjected personally to a danger of torture or to a risk to her life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment should she return to China.

The panel finds that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. Therefore, her claim is rejected.
